cases.name: TVS Accelerator
cases.title: The sales app was there. The sales team wasn't using it.
cases.summary: A dealership sales platform had a serious adoption problem. We went to the showroom floor to understand the workarounds, then redesigned the parts that mattered: enquiry capture and quotations.
cases.intro: A customer walks into a TVS showroom. The sales executive begins a conversation. A mobile app should make this easier—not compete for the customer's attention.
cases.context: TVS Accelerator supported the journey from enquiry through bookings, test rides and delivery. Sales executives needed speed; managers needed accurate, connected records. Too often, staff used paper because it was faster in the moment.
cases.problem: The issue wasn't simply an outdated interface. It was a workflow that asked for too much at the wrong moment, while the real work happened face to face.
cases.people: Sales executives wanted to stay engaged with customers. Branch managers wanted visibility into follow-ups and quotations. Dealer owners wanted consistent, comparable information.
cases.approach: We visited dealerships, observed sales conversations, interviewed executives and managers, prioritised with the business, then designed and tested the solutions in two-week sprints.
decisions: Observe the workaround
Paper was a tool users chose because it helped them stay present in the conversation.
Separate immediate from later
Capture enough to create an enquiry, then complete the details through follow-ups.
Make the digital quote useful
Let managers control prices and let executives send a quotation customers can keep.
stats: Reported digital enquiry logging across the series
Reported sales linked to an enquiry
cases.limits: The numbers are presented as reported project results from the previous portfolio. They cover different stages of work and should not be attributed to any single screen.
cases.reflection: The most important change wasn't persuading people to use the app. It was changing the app to work with the way people sell.

cases.name: Finding the friction
cases.title: The paper wasn't a habit. It was a workaround.
cases.summary: Before drawing screens, we visited the dealerships where the work happened. The findings shifted the brief from a visual refresh to changes in the sales journey.
cases.intro: We didn't start with a new interface. We started by watching what happened when a customer walked in.
cases.context: Dealership visits in Pune and Bengaluru showed sales executives juggling walk-ins, enquiries, test rides and quotes. Recording complete data in the app competed with the sales conversation.
cases.problem: Staff were protecting the customer interaction, not rejecting digital tools. A long form interrupted the conversation and paper was simply faster to reach for.
cases.people: Sales executives, branch managers and dealer owners needed different things: speed, visibility and consistency. Field visits revealed why a single rigid flow was working for none of them.
cases.approach: We conducted on-site observation, interviews and incognito visits, gathered the recurring pain points, and brought them back to the business. Impact versus effort helped align the team on what to change first.
decisions: Capture now, complete later
The enquiry form had to respect a live sales conversation.
Build in follow-up visibility
Managers still needed complete data, not a permanent collection of partial leads.
Prioritise rather than redesign everything
Quick Enquiry, digital quotation and delivery checklist became the key bets.
stats: Reported design and review sprint cadence
cases.limits: This research case study focuses on observed workarounds and prioritisation. No research participant count or quantified research uplift was provided; the adjacent screenshots show the resulting product direction.
cases.reflection: The best clue was the workaround itself. People were not behaving irrationally. They had found a way to serve customers faster.

cases.name: Quick Enquiry
cases.title: A ten-minute form had no place in a ten-minute conversation.
cases.summary: Quick Enquiry separated the few fields needed immediately from the details needed later. The work extended into records, reminders, follow-ups and booking gates.
cases.intro: Someone comes in to ask about a scooter. The executive needs to get their name, number and interest without turning away from the conversation.
cases.context: The original form asked for detailed information up front. Some sales executives wrote it on paper and entered it much later, if at all. Late or missed entries meant missed follow-ups and poor reporting.
cases.problem: Speed and completeness seemed like opposite goals. The redesign had to give sales staff a genuinely quick first step without depriving managers of the information needed downstream.
cases.people: Sales executives needed a fast, forgiving first interaction; managers needed follow-up data and a traceable lead record.
cases.approach: We mapped the fields, split the flow into basic capture and later completion, then considered its consequences across enquiry lists, tasks, status indicators, reminders and booking. The source boards include nine interface sequences.
decisions: Capture the minimum
Use the essential first-step fields rather than requiring everything at once.
Make incomplete visible
Incomplete enquiries remain actionable through follow-up tasks and clear status.
Protect downstream work
Before booking, the app requests the required missing details instead of silently discarding them.
stats: Reported digital enquiry logging at this stage
Reported sales linked to a logged enquiry
cases.limits: The source describes a quick first capture, with full completion later. Avoid presenting the 10-second figure as the time to complete the entire enquiry.
cases.reflection: Removing fields wasn't the whole solution. The difficult work was designing the system that makes 'later' reliable.

cases.name: Digital Quotations
cases.title: The quotation book won because it worked.
cases.summary: We learned that handwritten quotes felt quick and negotiable. The new flow combined manager-controlled pricing, digital sharing, and a record customers and staff could return to.
cases.intro: The paper quotation book wasn't just a relic. It gave executives freedom to discuss offers and adjust to the dealership's pricing. Digital had to earn its place.
cases.context: Manual quotes could take five to seven minutes, were difficult to track, and could be lost. Fixed digital prices also conflicted with varied dealership offers and regional costs.
cases.problem: The job was to keep the flexibility of paper, while making the output accurate, shareable and retrievable.
cases.people: Branch managers needed control over variants, accessories, charges and discounts; sales executives needed speed; customers needed a quote they could understand and access.
cases.approach: The redesigned journey connects lead capture with quote generation, WhatsApp sharing, multiple vehicle options, manager-controlled price templates and a customer-facing portal.
decisions: Let the branch own the numbers
Managers configure quotation particulars and relevant price adjustments.
Use WhatsApp as the handoff
Send a formatted quote into the channel customers already use.
Keep a retrievable history
A quotation remains attached to the enquiry instead of disappearing with a paper sheet.
stats: Reported time to produce/share a quotation
Reported digital enquiry logging at this stage
cases.limits: The prior case study reports these outcomes; the underlying analytics were not supplied here. Some screenshots depict customer self-registration and broader enquiry flows alongside the quotation work.
cases.reflection: Paper succeeded because it fit the sales moment. Digital won when it could do that and still make the outcome shareable and trackable.
